summary: A reply to a complaint in RFC 531 that the UCSB resource evaluators had not read the Resource Notebook before testing services. The author argues there was a misunderstanding about what the evaluators were trying to do and how that differs from the aims of the software repository idea.

plainLanguage.summary: Someone said the testers hadn't read the instructions. The testers write back to say that was a misunderstanding about their job.

subtitle: A defense of UCSB's approach to evaluating network resources.

tldr.problem: In RFC 531, Mark Padlipsky criticized the UCSB resource evaluation group for failing to consult existing documentation before testing network services, suggesting they had been careless or derelict in their work.
tldr.mechanism: John Pickens of UCSB responded that there was a misunderstanding about what the evaluators actually do. They follow a systematic process: read the Resource Notebook, consult online documentation at the NIC, check site-specific documentation, and only then contact technical liaisons if questions remain.
tldr.outcome: Pickens explained that UCSB evaluators investigate dynamic phenomena like help facilities, response time, and reliability, not just documentation, and that they have helped drive improvements at both local and remote sites.

facts.label: Evaluation focus
facts.value: Help facilities, response time, reliability, human engineering

today: RFC 545 documents early ARPANET quality assurance practices and resource evaluation methodology. It reflects the collaborative and sometimes contentious nature of early network community discussions about resource management and service quality.

sections.title: The Critique and Misunderstanding
sections.content:
Mark Padlipsky, in RFC 531 ("Feast or Famine"), had criticized the UCSB resource evaluators for apparently failing to consult the Resource Notebook before conducting remote login tests. John Pickens responded on behalf of the UCSB Computer Systems Laboratory, explaining that Padlipsky had misunderstood both the evaluators' methods and their role in the network.

Pickens clarified that the UCSB evaluation group was well-versed in the Resource Notebook, and that other factors were at play in the login incidents Padlipsky cited. For instance, the OLS (Multics) TELNET server at that time did not echo lowercase characters, which created confusion even after consulting documentation. Padlipsky's own technical liaison had experienced the same difficulty.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone said the testers were careless. The testers said that was not true and that the problem was actually with the computer system, not with them.

sections.title: The Evaluation Process
sections.content:
Pickens outlined the UCSB evaluators' systematic approach. The first step is to read the Resource Notebook. Questions that remain after consulting the Notebook are addressed by accessing online documentation, first at the NIC and then at the site being evaluated. Only if issues persist after consulting all available documentation do the evaluators contact a technical liaison, either online or by telephone, sometimes even purchasing appropriate user manuals when necessary.

This approach prioritizes the most publicly available documentation, resorting to personal contact only when advertised resources fail to answer questions. If technical liaisons prefer to serve as consultants to uninitiated users, the UCSB team is willing to adjust their approach accordingly.
sections.plainLanguage: They read the book, looked at the online manuals, then asked people if they still did not understand. They tried not to bother busy people unless they really had to.

sections.title: Beyond Documentation: Investigating User Experience
sections.content:
Pickens stressed that resource evaluators investigate far more than just documentation availability. They examine dynamic phenomena such as the quality of help facilities, the responsiveness and reliability of online consultation, system response time, machine reliability, and human engineering aspects of the user interface. In effect, they serve as "plain clothes inspectors" on behalf of UCSB users.

The goal is not just to list what exists, but to identify areas for improvement and communicate constructive feedback to sites. The evaluators acknowledge they are still learning how best to phrase critiques in a constructive rather than destructive way.
sections.plainLanguage: They did not just read about how a computer system was supposed to work. They tested whether it actually worked well and whether it was easy to use.

sections.title: Impact and Intent
sections.content: Pickens concluded by asserting that while the UCSB evaluators do not claim absolute efficiency, they do claim good intent and good results. They have spurred improvements at both local and remote network sites through their work. The team apologized for any instances where their previous reviews may have caused offense and committed to continuing to improve their approach.
sections.plainLanguage: They said they were trying to help and that the sites they tested often made improvements because of their feedback.
